ops._why: examples/01: SmallRye Health on /healthz and /readyz, Hibernate validate, Panache entity

paragraphs: Walk the code: config comes from the environment via MicroProfile Config (factor III): QUARKUS_DATASOURCE_JDBC_URL, the username and password and SERVICE_VERSION override application.properties, never a baked-in file. The two probes come from SmallRye Health (quarkus-smallrye-health), mapped to /healthz and /readyz in application.properties. /healthz is liveness (am I alive? if not, restart me) and never checks a dependency. /readyz is readiness (can I serve?) and includes the datasource check, so when the database is unreachable it answers 503 with status DOWN, which takes the pod out of rotation without killing it. The probe reads the status code, not the body: Kubernetes treats any answer from 200 to 399 as ready. Custom checks are @Liveness and @Readiness beans; Example 21 adds one for the drain.

Persistence is Hibernate ORM with Panache. The Order entity maps the table that db/init creates, and quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy=validate makes Hibernate check the mapping instead of owning the schema. The resource returns a DTO record, never the entity. Getting liveness vs readiness wrong is a top cause of cascading restarts, so stress the distinction. Maven with the quarkus-bom (platform 3.40.1) pins every dependency reproducibly.

@POST @Transactional                          // one JTA transaction around both rows
// ... sku and quantity from the request; status = "confirmed"
order.persistAndFlush();                   // the state change; created_at read back
event.payload = new OrderPlacedPayload(order.id, order.sku, order.quantity, order.status);

// No Kafka call on the request path: Debezium tails the WAL and publishes order.placed.
ops._why: examples/04: order and OutboxEvent entities persisted in one @Transactional method

paragraphs: The whole trick is the @Transactional method: the insert of the order row and the insert of the outbox row run in one JTA transaction, so they commit or roll back together. Both rows are Panache entities over tables that db/init creates, and the outbox payload is a record stored in a jsonb column with @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON). There is no Kafka call inside the request path: if the broker is down, the order still commits and the event ships later when Debezium tails the write-ahead log and relays the outbox row in commit order. This decouples request latency and availability from Kafka's.

Example 04 needs no outbox extension: the outbox is a small table (aggregate id, event type, JSON payload, created_at) mapped by a plain OutboxEvent entity, and a standard Debezium Postgres connector handles the CDC. The Debezium Outbox Event Router single-message transform unwraps the row into the event envelope on the connector side. The Debezium Quarkus outbox extension is not used: it brings its own table layout, and one table and one connector serve every language. The same commit-together discipline reappears in the saga appendix.

// STEPS = charge_payment, reserve_stock, book_shipping; each SagaStep also names its inverse
SagaEntity saga = SagaEntity.findById(sagaId, LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE);  // row lock
var result = stepExecutor.execute(step.name(), context);    // call the owning service
context.put(step.name(), result);              // accumulate output into the context
saga.stepIndex++;                              // one commit: state + log row
saga.status = "COMPENSATING";                  // hand off to the unwinder
ops._why: examples/17: one transaction per step, PESSIMISTIC_WRITE row lock, log row in the same commit

paragraphs: This is the DB-backed option made concrete with Panache, and the default choice when the team wants to own the transitions. Key ideas: one saga row, loaded with a PESSIMISTIC_WRITE lock (findById with a LockModeType) so two workers cannot advance the same saga concurrently. advanceOneStep runs in its own transaction, one step per transaction: the new context, the new step index and the saga_log row commit together, so a crash leaves either the old state or the new one. The context is a JSON column (@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON)) that accumulates each step's result, which the data-dependency slide builds on. A failed step logs the failure, marks the saga COMPENSATING and returns, and the caller runs the unwinder.

Recovery needs no special path: on startup the service loads the RUNNING sagas and calls advance() again, and the loop resumes from the stored step index. The managed alternative is Quarkus Flow, which provides this state machine, retries and timers out of the box; the data-dependency slide shows it.

ops.find: Compensate only completed steps, in reverse, with an idempotency key so a retry never double-refunds.
ops.repl: Compensate only completed steps, in reverse, and log every attempt; make each compensation idempotent so a retry never double-refunds.

paragraphs: The compensation logic. Each forward step names its inverse (SagaStep holds both), and the saga's step index says how many steps completed. We walk those steps in reverse, newest first, and run each compensation through the same step executor. Every attempt is written to saga_log in its own transaction, as compensate or failed, so a compensation that fails is recorded rather than skipped, and the saga ends COMPENSATED.

In production you would also make each compensating call idempotent on the receiving service, for example with a key built from the saga id and the step, so a retry can never double-refund a customer, and track per-step compensation status so a crash halfway resumes from the right place. This is why compensations are designed up front, as part of each step, not bolted on after. If you use Quarkus Flow instead, you model these as the workflow's try/catch compensation tasks and the engine drives the unwind.

paragraphs: Walk the blocks. Ports: the domain declares plain Java interfaces, a repository and an event publisher, and depends on nothing else. The use case, PlaceOrderUseCase, is a plain class with no jakarta or Quarkus import: it creates the aggregate, saves it through the port and publishes a domain event through the port. One CDI producer method is the only place the framework meets it. The outbound ports are implemented by adapters: a Panache-backed repository over an OrderEntity (the domain Order stays free of JPA) and a publisher that logs the event.

The driving adapters are thin. The REST resource turns the HTTP body into a command and calls the use case. The command-line adapter is a QuarkusApplication started under a profile that turns the HTTP server off, and it calls the same use case and the same repository. That's dependency inversion serving the boundary: protocols are replaceable, the domain stays stable.

ops.find: One SIGTERM flips readiness; after DRAIN_DELAY_SECONDS, Quarkus.asyncExit(0) drains in-flight HTTP within quarkus.shutdown.timeout (20 s).
ops.repl: One SIGTERM flips readiness; after quarkus.shutdown.delay (5 s) Quarkus stops HTTP and drains in-flight requests within quarkus.shutdown.timeout (20 s).

paragraphs: Example 21 lets Quarkus run the drain. With quarkus.shutdown.delay-enabled=true, one SIGTERM, the only signal Kubernetes sends before SIGKILL, makes Quarkus fire ShutdownDelayInitiatedEvent and keep serving for quarkus.shutdown.delay (DRAIN_DELAY_SECONDS, 5 s; it plays the part of a preStop sleep) while the endpoint removal propagates. The ShutdownState bean observes the event and flips its flag, so the DrainReadinessCheck, a SmallRye Health @Readiness check, reports DOWN and /readyz answers 503 beside the datasource check, while /healthz keeps answering 200.

When the delay ends Quarkus stops accepting connections, fires ShutdownEvent, waits for in-flight requests up to quarkus.shutdown.timeout (20 s), closes the datasource and exits, inside the 30-second grace period. A ShutdownEvent observer is also the hook for what Quarkus leaves to you: Kafka consumers, the scheduler, WebSockets. Pair it with the Kubernetes side: probes, preStop and the grace period.

ops._why: examples/24: typed REST Client for legacy, Jackson-serialized event map, cache-aside on a raw body

paragraphs: The Quarkus decorator. LegacyClient is a typed MicroProfile REST Client (quarkus.rest-client.legacy.url), so the call to the legacy service is a method call. The POST path delegates the write to the legacy service, which stays the source of truth, reads the new order id from its answer and emits an order.placed event through a Reactive Messaging Emitter on the order-events-out channel. The event is a map written by the Jackson serializer, so the field order stays event, order_id, then the request fields. The GET path looks in Redis through the Quarkus Redis client (RedisDataSource, quarkus-redis-client), falls back to the legacy service on a miss and populates the cache with a 60-second TTL; the log lines CACHE_HIT and CACHE_MISS show which way it went.
The legacy service does not know it is wrapped, and clients do not know they talk to a decorator.

Over time more behaviour moves into the decorator: validation rules, idempotency keys, deduplication, multi-source reads. To retire the legacy service, implement the order storage inside the decorator (or in a new service it calls) and stop forwarding; the API stays the same for clients.

paragraphs: Quarkus cache-aside, as Example 25 runs it. SafeRedis wraps the Quarkus Redis client so every call is best effort: a Redis failure is logged and the read falls through to the database. The GET path looks in Redis for ca:product:<id>, falls back to Store.findProduct, a Panache lookup in its own transaction, on a miss and populates the cache with a 60-second TTL; the response says whether the value came from the cache or the db. The PUT path updates the row in a transaction and then deletes the cache key; setting the new value instead is write-through.
For high-cardinality keys, set a maxmemory-policy on Redis (allkeys-lru is typical) so the cache cannot grow without bound.

ops.find: @CacheResult turns the method body into a loader. Callers see one interface; the cache miss path is invisible.
ops.repl: Cache.get turns the lookup into a loader call: the cache owns the miss path, and a flag in the loader reports where the value came from.

paragraphs: Read-through in Quarkus uses the Cache API from quarkus-cache with quarkus-redis-cache behind it. Cache.get(key, loader) looks in Redis first and runs the loader only on a miss, then stores the result for the TTL (quarkus.cache.redis.read-through.expire-after-write) under the configured prefix, so the application holds no if/else around the cache. The cache needs the value type (quarkus.cache.redis.read-through.value-type) to read entries back. A flag set inside the loader tells the response whether the value came from the cache or the database.

A loader that throws, for a missing product, caches nothing, and when Redis is unreachable Cache.get runs the loader and returns its value, so a Redis outage costs hits, not availability. The annotation form, @CacheResult on a service method, expresses the same pattern declaratively; the explicit call is used here because the response reports the source of the value.

lines: public Response writeThroughUpdate(@RestPath String pid, ProductUpdate body) {
store.updateProduct(pid, body.name(), body.priceCents());  // 1. DB first (source of truth)
Product row = store.findProduct(pid);                      //    read back the stored row
cache.setex("wt:product:" + pid, toJson(row), ttl);    // 2. cache second: SET
ops._why: examples/25: write the database first, then SET the cache with the stored row

paragraphs: Write-through in Quarkus. The update writes the row first, then reads it back through Store.findProduct and caches that value: the canonical row, including server-side defaults. The DB write comes first because the DB is the source of truth; if the cache write fails, you lose cache freshness, not data.

Writing the request body straight to the cache would save a read but can diverge from the row when the database applies defaults, triggers or computed columns. The TTL is the safety net: if cache and DB drift briefly, they converge when the entry expires and the next read repopulates it.

lines: // 1. SIGTERM: Quarkus fires ShutdownDelayInitiatedEvent and keeps serving for the delay
// 2. the delay keeps serving while the load balancer stops routing
// 3. delay over: HTTP stops, in-flight requests drain, ShutdownEvent fires
// 4. Quarkus closes the pools and the process exits
ops._why: Appendix M recap follows examples/21 (one SIGTERM, delay, 20 s drain)

paragraphs: Example 21 lets Quarkus run the drain: quarkus.shutdown.delay-enabled, quarkus.shutdown.delay and quarkus.shutdown.timeout. On the single SIGTERM: (1) Quarkus fires ShutdownDelayInitiatedEvent and an observer flips the ShutdownState flag, so the SmallRye Health readiness check reports DOWN, /readyz answers 503 and Kubernetes stops routing new traffic, while /healthz stays 200; (2) the delay keeps the service serving, so the load balancer's removal propagates; (3) when it ends, Quarkus stops HTTP and drains in-flight requests within quarkus.shutdown.timeout (20 s); (4) Quarkus closes the datasource and the process exits. Appendix H covers the Kubernetes-side preStop and terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
